premise: A drama set inside NASA Mission Control across the four days of Apollo 13, from the oxygen-tank rupture to splashdown in April 1970.
title: APOLLO 13 · 1970
overview: The research reconstructs the physical and bureaucratic environment of NASA Mission Operations Control Room 2 during the Apollo 13 crisis in April 1970. Flight controllers operated inside a dim, windowless facility reliant on CRT displays, mainframe data streams, paper calculations, and dense audio loop networks. The crisis forced multiple shifts of engineers to improvise survival procedures under continuous operational stress. This film follows the controllers who realize their own earlier testing oversights directly contributed to the spacecraft tank failure. They must confront their professional culpability while working to bring the crew back alive.

boxes.name: CONSOLE HARDWARE ARCHITECTURE
boxes.description: Gather engineering schematics, CRT screen phosphor colors, illuminated push-button specs, and Pneumatic tube routing inside the Manned Spacecraft Center Building 30 Mission Operations Control Room.
boxes.rationale: The production must fabricate dozens of functional period telemetry consoles to sustain spatial continuity across continuous four-day set-bound scenes.
boxes.summary: Building 30 housed the Mission Operations Control Room on its second and third floors. Controllers monitored operations through custom console housings fitted with CRT monitors and illuminated push-button arrays. Pneumatic tubes routed physical paperwork, flight plan updates, and telemetry printouts across the room. Operational documentation from the era details exact panel wiring schematics and display switch configurations. The consoles provided fixed station assignments for telemetry oversight across every phase of the mission.

boxes.name: COMMUNICATIONS LOOP ACOUSTICS
boxes.description: Catalog audio tapes of the internal flight director, capcom, backroom trench, and recovery voice loops to transcribe cadences and audio fidelity variations.
boxes.rationale: Sound designers require the precise frequency cutoffs and squelch tones of 1970 communications headsets to construct an accurate auditory environment.
boxes.summary: Controllers communicated across multiple specialized audio channels, including the flight director, Capcom, and trench loops. Real-time recordings preserve the precise cadences and technical shorthand spoken during the mission. Backroom staff channeled analysis to front-row flight controllers using distinct ground-to-air and internal lines. These loop recordings document the shift changes, procedural debates, and audio dropouts that occurred across the four days. The technical speech patterns were clipped, rapid, and tightly regulated by procedure.

boxes.name: ENGINEERING DIVISION DEMOGRAPHICS
boxes.description: Survey personnel files, educational histories, home regions, and military veteran ratios of the flight controllers on duty during April 1970.
boxes.rationale: The casting team needs precise age profiles and regional physical types to assemble an authentic ensemble of young government engineers.
boxes.summary: The flight control team consisted primarily of young civilian engineers, system specialists, and military veterans. Detailed personnel rosters show many controllers were recruited straight out of regional engineering universities. Flight controllers handled dedicated positions such as GUIDO, EECOM, and RETRO. Their average age was under thirty during the lunar landing missions. The personnel files document their educational paths, aerospace backgrounds, and assignments within the flight control division.

boxes.name: SHIFT ROTATION ATTIRE
boxes.description: Collect archival photographs showing the progressive rumpling, sweat patterns, necktie looseness, and cigarette burns on controllers' short-sleeve shirts across eighty-four consecutive hours.
boxes.rationale: Costumers need photographic proof of fabric degradation to track the physical exhaustion of staff over four sleepless days.
boxes.summary: Archival photographs record the progressive deterioration of controller attire across the eighty-four-hour crisis. Men wore short-sleeved white button-down shirts, dark neckties, and slacks. Over multiple continuous shifts, ties loosened, collars wilted, and sweat stains appeared. Flight controllers remained stationed at their consoles through extended shifts without changing clothes. The surviving photography captures crumpled fabrics and exhausted postures across the control room.

boxes.name: CONTROL ROOM CONSUMABLES
boxes.description: Document the precise brands of instant coffee, vending machine pastries, tobacco, ashtrays, paper cup prints, and takeout food containers present in the facility during the crisis.
boxes.rationale: Set dressers must populate console desks with accurate physical debris to indicate the passage of exhausting time.
boxes.summary: Mission Control consoles accumulated consumer packaging and food detritus throughout the operation. Controllers consumed commercial cigarettes, coffee poured into paper cups, and vending machine pastries. Heavy glass and metal ashtrays sat directly on console surfaces alongside official flight manuals. Food service logs and historical photos record takeout containers brought in during off-hours rotations. Trash accumulated around desk spaces as controllers worked through the emergency.

boxes.name: TECHNICAL CRISIS VOCABULARY
boxes.description: Transcribe the specialized telemetry shorthand, mathematical abbreviations, acronyms, and informal floor jargon used by mission controllers during life-support anomalies.
boxes.rationale: Writers need exact technical phrasing so dialogue remains authentic during high-stress problem-solving sequences.
boxes.summary: Flight controllers relied on an extensive vocabulary of acronyms, telemetry codes, and operational jargon. Specialized terms covered trajectory adjustments, spacecraft electrical busses, and consumable life-support margins. Manuals codified abbreviations for positions like GUIDO, EECOM, and RETRO, as well as tracking stations worldwide. Malfunction procedures established shorthand protocols for immediate troubleshooting during subsystem failures. Controllers spoke entirely in these terms when reporting anomalies over internal loops.

boxes.name: FACILITY LIGHTING PROTOCOLS
boxes.description: Determine the exact foot-candle levels, fluorescent tube color temperatures, projector screen luminance, and darkness protocols maintained in the Operations Control Room.
boxes.rationale: The cinematographer must match authentic lighting ratios between glow-in-the-dark console displays and cavernous overhead fixtures.
boxes.summary: The Operations Control Room maintained low interior ambient light levels to ensure visibility of CRT consoles and wall projections. Fluorescent ceiling fixtures were dimmed according to strict operational facility protocols. Forward wall screens displayed orbital tracks, system statuses, and world maps using rear-projection systems. Engineers checked console lighting levels using established foot-candle standards for control centers. The resulting atmosphere placed console stations in semi-darkness beneath illuminated monitors.

boxes.name: CLEAR LAKE COMMUTING
boxes.description: Photograph the access highways, parking lots, security gates, police checkpoints, and personal vehicle models driven by NASA personnel around Clear Lake, Texas in 1970.
boxes.rationale: Location managers must secure accurate period parking facilities and mid-century access roads for peripheral facility shots.
boxes.summary: Controllers commuted to the Manned Spacecraft Center across access roads and highways around Clear Lake, Texas. The surrounding suburban landscape featured wide access routes, flat terrain, and open employee parking lots. Personnel passed through federal security checkpoints and entry gates when reporting to Building 30. Archival records document the access routes connecting the isolated suburban campus with the greater Houston area. Daily traffic consisted of standard American passenger vehicles from the late 1960s.

boxes.name: PRESS CORPS INFRASTRUCTURE
boxes.description: Examine the layout of the adjacent MSC Building 1 auditorium press center, including broadcast television camera positions, teletype machines, and payphone banks.
boxes.rationale: The art department must recreate the institutional media spaces where outside civic pressure converged on NASA staff.
boxes.summary: MSC Building 1 housed the central auditorium press center dedicated to print and broadcast journalists. The facility contained television camera platforms, teletype machines, and banks of public payphones for wire reporters. Press site handbooks detailed how briefings and mission status reports were coordinated for external media. Correspondents filed immediate reports from designated workspace areas located adjacent to the control complex. NASA public affairs teams operated directly from this auditorium to release crew status statements.

boxes.name: OFFICE OF CIVILIAN DEFENSE RELATIONS
boxes.description: Collect records regarding Houston area police details, federal site security procedures, and domestic political protest monitoring around the aerospace complex during the Vietnam War era.
boxes.rationale: The script department must ground the insular federal facility within the contentious domestic politics of the spring of 1970.
boxes.summary: Local law enforcement worked alongside federal security personnel to monitor the Manned Spacecraft Center perimeter during 1970. Houston police departments coordinated regional traffic details and off-site protective measures. Federal record groups preserve the operational relationship between regional civil authorities and NASA facility security during the Vietnam War period. Security details maintained monitoring of public demonstrations and political unrest that occurred near aerospace installations. Access to technical buildings remained restricted by guard teams.

boxes.name: SUPPORT STAFF TRENCH DYNAMICS
boxes.description: Analyze the organizational hierarchy, desk-level workspace arrangements, and real-time calculation procedures of the Staff Support Rooms (backrooms) feeding data to the front trench.
boxes.rationale: It bridges internal voice communications, crisis vocabulary shorthand, console hardware ergonomics, and controller staffing demographics during the four-day emergency.
boxes.summary: Staff Support Rooms operated directly behind the primary control floor, functioning as the backrooms for each discipline. Support engineers gathered raw data, verified calculations, and channeled technical recommendations forward to the trench. Auxiliary computing facilities provided supplementary processing power for complex orbital maneuvers. Historical diagrams show close-quarters desk layouts where teams worked out contingency numbers by hand. The front trench flight controllers depended entirely on the analytical output of these backroom staff.

boxes.name: MANUAL CALCULATION TOOLS
boxes.description: Catalog the specific slide rules, graphing papers, manual plotters, grease pencils, and desk calculators used by controllers to verify orbital trajectories and power budgets when primary computer telemetry failed.
boxes.rationale: Physical calculation instruments directly interface with console layouts, backroom workflow dynamics, technical vocabulary, and character hand-props during the power-down sequence.
boxes.summary: Controllers relied on manual calculation tools to verify spacecraft orbital state vectors and power lifetimes. Pocket slide rules such as the Pickett N600-ES were kept at console desks for rapid calculations. Engineers plotted trajectory curves manually using graph paper, drafting tools, and grease pencils. Electronic desk calculators and specialized paper templates supplemented mainframe computer outputs during contingency planning. These physical calculation tools served as direct backups when digital displays malfunctioned.

boxes.name: REAL-TIME TELEMETRY DATA FLOW
boxes.description: Trace the physical and digital trajectory of telemetry data from deep-space tracking stations through mainframe computers to control room display screens and plotting boards.
boxes.rationale: It links console hardware, support backrooms, manual calculation tools, and technical vocabulary by defining how critical spacecraft data physically entered and moved through the facility during the anomaly.
boxes.summary: Spacecraft telemetry flowed through the global Manned Space Flight Network of ground tracking stations to Mission Control. Telemetry and tracking data traveled from overseas antennas through the Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland. Mainframe computers at the Houston center processed the incoming bitstreams into readable engineering units. The processed telemetry was then routed to individual console CRT screens and automated wall plotting displays. Ground controllers depended on this fixed data chain to monitor the health of all onboard spacecraft systems.

### **PREFACE**

### The National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) selected the first group of astronauts in 1959. From 500 candidates having the required jet aircraft flight experience and engineering training as well as height below 5 feet 11 inches, 7 military men became the Nation's first astronauts. MOCR - Manned Spaceflight Operations Association. # MOCR

The second and third floors of Building 30 each contain a Mission Operations Control Room (MOCR), pronounced “mouker”. The second floor contains MOCR 1 and the third floor contains MOCR 2; the National Historic Landmark now called the Apollo Mission Control Center. The two MOCRs are not identical and they changed roles, as well as configurations during Gemini, Apollo, Apollo-Soyuz, Skylab and the Space Shuttle. The whole building complex changed again after the Shuttle Program was cancelled and the operations shifted to the International Space Station. See the Positions section for the consoles that were in MOCR 2 during the lunar landing missions.

Johnson Space Center National Aeronautics and Space Administration
National Historic Landmark (NHL) Status Due to its impactfulness and criticality to human spaceflight in America, Building 30 -- The Christopher C. Kraft, Jr. Mission Control Center-- became a National Historic Landmark (NHL) in1985.
Control Room In the center is the iconic Mission Operations Control Room, often referred to as the “MOCR,” with the consoles used by the various flight controllers.
• Consoles: All consoles were restored-- not painted-- to the Apollo
era, specifically Apollo15, representing the apex of technological achievement of the Apollo Missions.
Original documents were copied for display.
• Displays and Clocks: The large group displays on the west wall of
the MOCR were restored with appropriate projection technology to recreate Apollo-era use of the screens. Of the nine original timing screens, five were restored and four were procured from the companies that originally manufactured them.
Summary Projection Room “Bat Cave”
At the front of the room are large group display screens; behind these screens is the Summary Display Projection Room, sometimes referred to as the “Bat Cave.” Here, maps and images were projected onto the screens, many with illuminated, electromechanical plotter overlays

**Space Food**

Many people ask NASA about what and how the astronauts eat

eat are not provided in tubes and they are neither bland nor

how food systems and menu items have evolved, what and how

astronauts in space eat now and what future voyagers may eat.

**History**

The food that NASA’s early astronauts had to eat in space is a

testament to their fortitude. John Glenn, America’s first man to eat

anything in the near-weightless environment of Earth orbit, found

the task of eating fairly easy, but found the menu to be limited.

Other Mercury astronauts had to endure bite-sized cubes, freeze-

dried powders and semi-liquids packaged in aluminum tubes.

The mission of Records Division is to function in a supporting role to the patrol and investigative divisions. 2. Don't Know What a Slide Rule Is For
Of course the designers also used digital computers, but in the 1960s computers were giant machines that you programmed with punched cards, and they were strictly reserved for only the most complex mathematical calculations.
As the 40th anniversary of the Apollo 11 mission approaches, we are constantly reminded of how incredible that voyage was. Add to the incredulity the slide rule : the basic mathematical tool that helped get the astronauts to the moon and back.
The visitors who gathered around the Command Module on Space Day generally fell into two camps.
For this presentation, I got out the manual and taught myself all over again how to use it. It was not easy.
The National Air and Space Museum has preserved a few slide rules, including one carried by Apollo 13 astronauts on their April 1970 journey.

# How NASA Restored Its Historic Apollo Mission Control Center

The historic control center at the heart of the Apollo 11 moon landing was almost lost to neglect. Then a retired flight director got involved.

By Melissa Dalton April 12, 2023

The restoration project focused on accuracy, right down to the brand of cigarettes left at each console.

Image: Courtesy NASA

### Failure is Not an Option - Gene Kranz

Spaceflight operations presents a unique range of challenges unlike those found on earth. Time, distance, and the remote environment provide a unique opportunity to assess planning, training and operations of the integrated crew ground team. Leadership, trust, values and teamwork provide the foundation for the compelling story of early space missions concluding with the rescue of the Apollo 13 crew after an oxygen tank exploded with the spacecraft 200,000 miles from earth. The story concludes with a summary of the technical cause of the explosion. Like an aircraft accident, the Apollo 13 tank explosion required a series of apparently unrelated events none of which by itself would have caused the failure.

prior_art.premise: A drama set inside NASA Mission Control across the four days of Apollo 13, from the oxygen-tank rupture to splashdown in April 1970.

neighbors.title: Apollo 13
neighbors.overview: The true story of technical troubles that scuttle the Apollo 13 lunar mission in 1970, risking the lives of astronaut Jim Lovell and his crew, with the failed journey turning into a thrilling saga of heroism. Drifting more than 200,000 miles from Earth, the astronauts work furiously with the ground crew to avert tragedy.
neighbors.engine: exploited mechanical flaw in the oxygen system

neighbors.title: Salyut-7
neighbors.overview: USSR, June 1985. After contact with the Salyut 7 space station is lost, cosmonauts Vladimir Dzhanibekov and Viktor Savinykh dock with the empty, frozen craft, and bring her back to life. Based on actual events.
neighbors.engine: exploited electrical flaw in station hardware
neighbors.moral_arc: loyalty to comrades redeems political coercion

neighbors.title: The Right Stuff
neighbors.overview: At the dawn of the Space Race, seven test pilots set out to become the first American astronauts to enter space. However, the road to making history brings momentous challenges.
neighbors.engine: exploited psychological flaw in institutional hubris

neighbors.title: The Real Right Stuff
neighbors.overview: The story of America's first astronauts, known as the Mercury 7, told through archival news & radio reports, newly transferred & previously unheard NASA mission audio recordings, and more rare & unseen material.
neighbors.engine: exploited historical record shipped as archival media
neighbors.moral_arc: collective effort secures a national achievement

neighbors.title: First Man
neighbors.overview: A look at the life of the astronaut, Neil Armstrong, and the legendary space mission that led him to become the first man to walk on the Moon on July 20, 1969.
neighbors.engine: exploited emotional flaw of unexpressed grief
neighbors.moral_arc: private sorrow finds release through professional endurance
neighbors.ending: mission completed with silent personal reconciliation

neighbors.title: The Martian
neighbors.overview: During a manned mission to Mars, Astronaut Mark Watney is presumed dead after a fierce storm and left behind by his crew. But Watney has survived and finds himself stranded and alone on the hostile planet. With only meager supplies, he must draw upon his ingenuity, wit and spirit to subsist and find a way to signal to Earth that he is alive.
neighbors.engine: exploited scientific ingenuity shipped as standard equipment

neighbors.title: Hidden Figures
neighbors.overview: The untold story of Katherine G. Johnson, Dorothy Vaughan and Mary Jackson – brilliant African-American women working at NASA and serving as the brains behind one of the greatest operations in history – the launch of astronaut John Glenn into orbit. The visionary trio crossed all gender and race lines to inspire generations to dream big.
neighbors.engine: exploited systemic bias flaw in workplace hierarchy
neighbors.ending: ground calculations validate the orbital trajectory

neighbors.title: Love
neighbors.overview: After losing contact with Earth, Astronaut Lee Miller becomes stranded in orbit alone aboard the International Space Station. As time passes and life support systems dwindle, Lee battles to maintain his sanity - and simply stay alive. His world is a claustrophobic and lonely existence, until he makes a strange discovery aboard the ship.
neighbors.engine: exploited psychological isolation flaw in prolonged confinement

neighbors.title: First Man into Space
neighbors.overview: The first pilot to leave Earth's atmosphere lands, then vanishes; but something with a craving for blood prowls the countryside...
neighbors.engine: exploited biological mutation flaw caused by cosmic radiation
neighbors.ending: dying monster provides crucial scientific data

neighbors.title: The Devil's Mouth
neighbors.overview: A group of college friends' Thailand adventure turns deadly when they become trapped in submerged caves with a dangerous predator. As oxygen runs low, past conflicts emerge in their desperate fight for survival.
neighbors.engine: exploited physical vulnerability flaw in a trapped environment

neighbors.title: Santo vs. the Martian Invasion
neighbors.overview: In this Mexican sci-fi fantasy, big beefy Martians invade the earth. Ostensibly, they have come to warn people about the dangers of nuclear testing and exploring space, but their real mission becomes manifest when they begin using their special powers and gadgets to exploit weak earthlings.
neighbors.engine: exploited alien invasion feature shipped as advanced weaponry

neighbors.title: It All Adds Up - The Making of Hidden Figures
neighbors.overview: It All Adds Up is an above average set of featurettes that kind of ping pongs between more traditional EPK fare with interviews and a more thoughtful analysis of some of the actual history involved.
neighbors.engine: exploited promotional commentary shipped as retrospective access
